name: swift-collections (Heap)
baseline: Re-sorting an Array (or scanning it with min()/max()) to get the smallest or largest element
verdict_reason: The documentation publishes only absolute per-operation timings for Heap itself, as a chart image, with no comparison against sorting an Array or against another priority queue. The advantage over re-sorting follows from O(log n) versus O(n log n) complexity, but no published number measures it.
tier_reason: Numbers exist only in a chart image with no baseline series; text gives complexities and the test machine.
claimed_speedup: No comparative numbers. Documented complexity is O(log n) insert and removal and O(1) min and max; the chart of absolute per-element times was generated in release mode on a 16-inch 2019 MacBook Pro with a 2.3 GHz 8-Core Intel Core i9.
workload: Heap<Int>: init from range, insert, insert(contentsOf:), popMin, popMax; 1 to 1M elements (chart).
hardware: MacBook Pro (16-inch, 2019), 2.3 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9
toolchain: Release mode; Swift version not stated
platforms: All Swift platforms: iOS, macOS, tvOS, watchOS, visionOS, Linux, Windows
one_liner: Apple's array-backed min-max heap for priority queues; O(log n) push and pop instead of re-sorting an Array.
how_it_is_fast: Heap is an implicit min-max heap stored in a single contiguous array: even levels are min levels, odd levels are max levels. Insert and removal walk one root-to-leaf path, so they cost O(log n), and both the minimum and the maximum are readable in O(1).
use_it_when: Priority queues, schedulers, Dijkstra or A* open sets
Code that appends and then re-sorts an Array, or calls min() on every step, to pull the next item
You need both ends: popMin and popMax on one structure
skip_it_when: You need all elements in sorted order once: a single sort() is simpler and usually faster
Very small queues where a linear min() scan is already cheap
You need stable ordering among equal priorities: heaps do not preserve insertion order
caveats: Numbers exist only in a chart image (Documentation/Images/Heap Performance.png) with no comparison series.
Measured in 2021 on an Intel MacBook Pro; Swift version not stated.
The PR history shows reference benchmarks against CFBinaryHeap and std::priority_queue were added to the benchmark suite, but their results are not published in text.
tradeoffs: Not a Sequence: iteration order is not sorted unless you pop elements
Min-max levels make each operation do a little more comparison work than a plain binary heap

evidence.quote: | Insert | O(log n) | | Get smallest element | O(1) | | Get largest element | O(1) | | Remove smallest element | O(log n) | | Remove largest element | O(log n) |
The above graph was generated in release mode on a MacBook Pro (16-inch, 2019) with a 2.3 GHz 8-Core Intel Core i9 using the benchmarks defined in the `swift-collections-benchmark` target.
